analysis.one_liner: Taxes more merged-and-offshored US companies as domestic corporations so they keep paying US taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: introduced with 15 cosponsors in January 2015, it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a US company merges with a smaller foreign company and renames itself abroad to escape US taxes — a practice called a corporate inversion — the bill would make it keep paying US corporate taxes. Under current law that only happens if the merged company ends up mostly owned by the old US shareholders at a very high threshold; the bill lowers that threshold to 50% and also catches companies whose executives and day-to-day management stay in the United States. It applies to deals completed after May 8, 2014.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who otherwise absorb the revenue lost when profitable companies move their paper headquarters abroad; and US-based companies that stay and pay taxes without getting an advantage handed to rivals that invert.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and companies that stay

how_it_helps.text: Treats a foreign company that acquires a US company as a US taxpayer if former US shareholders own more than 50% of it, or if the group's management and control stays primarily in the United States with significant domestic business activity (at least 25% of employees, payroll, assets, or income in the US) [S2] [S3].
Closes the gap in current law, which triggers the tax only when the ownership threshold is much higher, leaving room for deals designed to fall just below it [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: US companies that had planned or completed mergers to reincorporate in low-tax foreign countries; their shareholders would face higher US tax bills on the combined company's income.
analysis.who_pays_short: US companies inverting through foreign mergers

drawbacks.text: A company whose former US shareholders hold 50% or less after the deal would still escape US taxation, so the bill narrows the loophole rather than eliminating it [S3].

The bill keeps an exception for companies with substantial business activities in the country of reincorporation, and in 2015 US corporate tax rates were widely criticized as uncompetitive, an argument that companies said drove inversions in the first place (general knowledge).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real tax avoidance practice and would raise revenue from companies that remain managed and mostly owned in the US, though it leaves room for deals engineered just under its thresholds and does not address the tax-code design issues companies cited as their motive.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on January 20, 2015, with original cosponsors including Sens. Reed, Whitehouse, Warren, Hirono, Franken, Feinstein, and Boxer [S1] [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, the only action ever recorded on it [S5].
The bill gathered 15 cosponsors — 14 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republicans [S4].
With no hearing, markup, or vote, it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational companies that used or planned foreign mergers to reduce their US tax bills kept the current-law treatment the bill would have ended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that inverted to cut their US taxes

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Corporate Inversions Act of 2015 in the Senate.

for.name: 15 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 14 Democrats and 1 Independent cosponsoring the bill

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to, chaired by a Republican, which never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after it was referred on January 20, 2015.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Held the Senate majority and the Finance Committee chair during the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Brought no corporate-inversion tax legislation matching this approach to the floor in the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sen. Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Finance Committee never acted.

industries.note: These companies merge with smaller foreign firms and move their legal address abroad to lower US taxes; the bill would tax the resulting companies as domestic when US owners keep 50% or more of the stock or management stays in the US. Ordinary taxpayers otherwise make up the revenue these arrangements avoid [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: US-headquartered companies that pay full US taxes
industries.note: By reducing the tax advantage of inverting, the bill levels the field for companies that stay, whose competitiveness relative to inverted rivals improves [S2] [S3].
